evidence_quotes.quote: This paper describes the institutions and negotiating arenas through which indigenous peoples of these two countries seek to define, increase or influence their access to water, and the legitimacy of their water related values, ethics, and practices.
This paper describes the customary water governance systems of two neighbouring countries, Australia and East Timor, each at a different stage in modernising and reforming their water sectors.

The next section defines customary water governance systems; then case studies describe these systems in Australia and East Timor. An overview of the recent sectoral reforms in the two countries is then provided, with a description of some Indigenous and local responses to these changes and policy interventions in each country.
Federal and state governments reformed their water statutes to implement the NWI; however, there is no easily identifiable Australian model of water resource legislation.

For example, at the same time as it recognises a role for tara bandu, the law also proposes designating legal “owners” for all elements of the water supply system and imposing a state cost recovery tariff on water use (Ministry of Infrastructure, 2010). It is unclear what the implications of these measures will be for extant customary systems of water resource use and sharing.

criterion_notes.c1: Focuses on macro water-resource governance, catchment allocation, market-based water trading, rice-field irrigation rituals, environmental conservation, and customary waterscape rights rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (aside from briefly summarizing secondary ADB reports and draft national water supply policy in East Timor on PDF pp. 13-15).
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, yes: the paper discusses statutory water laws, property-rights reforms, Native Title Act 1993, the National Water Initiative, East Timor's 2004 Water Services Decree and 2012 Draft Water Resources Law, and customary governance (tara bandu). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, no: the analysis addresses macro water-resource allocation, environmental conservation management, and customary natural-resource governance rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access (only noting in passing on PDF p. 15 that East Timor's draft law proposes designating legal owners and imposing a cost-recovery tariff, without analyzing its operation on service access).
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical study design, methodology, sample, or primary empirical data are reported, and the article is not a systematic empirical synthesis; it is a comparative narrative policy and institutional essay synthesizing published literature, statutes, and draft policy documents.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report primary or synthesized empirical outcomes measuring household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the paper is a non-empirical comparative policy overview, no empirical study population, sample, unit of analysis, or analytical exposure-outcome design for service access can be identified.

study_design: Comparative narrative policy and literature overview (non-empirical essay)
exposure: Statutory water-resource governance and allocation reforms interacting with Indigenous customary water governance systems
rationale: Excluded as E05 (no empirical evidence). This article is a comparative narrative policy and conceptual overview of statutory water-resource reforms and Indigenous customary water governance in Australia and East Timor, synthesizing secondary literature, statutes, and draft policy documents without any empirical research design, methods, sample, or primary empirical data. Substantively, it also examines river-basin/aquifer resource allocation, irrigation, and customary waterscape conservation rather than empirical household or community water or sanitation service access outcomes.
